essays.stem: Describe the equipment needed to produce a basic mechanical drawing by hand, and say what each item is used for.
essays.modelAnswer: A drawing board with a smooth surface holds the paper, which is fixed with drafting tape or clips. A T-square slides along the edge of the board to draw horizontal lines and to guide the set squares. A 45° set square and a 30°/60° set square are used for vertical lines and for lines at 30°, 45° and 60°. A scale rule is used to measure and to draw to scales such as 1:2 and 1:5. Pencils of different grades are needed: a hard 2H pencil for light construction lines and an HB or H pencil for outlines and lettering. A compass draws circles and arcs, and dividers transfer and step off distances. A protractor measures angles that the set squares cannot give. A circle template and a French curve help with small circles and smooth curves. A clean eraser, an erasing shield and a soft brush keep the drawing clean.
markingPoints: Drawing board and T-square — fixing the paper, horizontal lines, guiding the set squares
Set squares (45° and 30°/60°) and protractor — vertical and angled lines
Scale rule — measuring and drawing to scale
Pencil grades (2H construction, HB or H outlines) and eraser or brush
Compass and dividers (and templates or French curve) — circles, arcs, transferring distances

essays.stem: Explain the difference between first-angle and third-angle orthographic projection, and describe how the views are arranged in each.
essays.modelAnswer: Both methods show a part in flat views, each one looking straight at one side: usually the front view (elevation), the plan (top view) and an end view. The difference is where each view is placed on the sheet. In first-angle projection, each view is drawn on the far side of the object from where you look. So the plan, seen from above, is drawn below the front view, and the view seen from the left is drawn on the right of the front view. In third-angle projection, each view is drawn on the same side that it is seen from. The plan goes above the front view, and the view from the right goes on the right of the front view. In both methods the views are lined up with projection lines, and the same sizes line up across the views. The projection symbol, a cone shown in two views, must be drawn in or near the title block so that the reader knows which method has been used.
markingPoints: Both use flat views (front, plan, end) lined up with projection lines
First angle: plan drawn below the front view
First angle: view from the left drawn on the right
Third angle: plan above the front view, view from the right on the right
Projection symbol shown so the reader knows which method

essays.stem: Describe the steps to produce a three-view orthographic drawing of a simple welded bracket on A3 paper, from setting up the sheet to lining in.
essays.modelAnswer: Fix the A3 sheet square on the board using the T-square, and tape the corners. Draw the border and the title block. Work out the space each view needs at the chosen scale, and the gaps between the views, so that the drawing is centred on the sheet. Using a 2H pencil and light construction lines, block in the overall shape of the front view first. Project lines across and up or down with the T-square and set squares to block in the plan and the end view, in the right places for first-angle or third-angle projection. Add details such as holes, chamfers and weld positions in every view where they show, with centre lines through the holes. Check all the sizes against the sketch or model. Then line in the visible outlines with a firm, thick HB line, the hidden edges with thin dashes and the centre lines with thin chain lines. Add the dimensions, notes and projection symbol, fill in the title block, and clean off loose construction lines.
markingPoints: Sheet fixed square; border and title block drawn
Views spaced and centred to suit the scale
Light construction lines; front view first, the others projected in the correct places
Details and centre lines added, and sizes checked
Lined in with the correct line types; dimensions, notes, symbol and title block completed

essays.stem: Explain the main rules for dimensioning a mechanical drawing so that it is clear and easy to use in the workshop.
essays.modelAnswer: All sizes are in millimetres, with a note such as ALL DIMENSIONS IN MM, so the unit is not written after each number. Dimensions show the real size of the part, whatever the scale of the drawing. Each size is shown once only, and every size needed to make the part is given, so nobody has to measure the drawing or add up sizes. Dimensions are placed outside the views where possible, on the view that shows the feature most clearly, and not on hidden lines. Dimension lines and projection lines are thin, with a small gap between the projection line and the outline, and the projection line goes a little past the dimension line. Arrowheads are neat and touch the projection lines. Numbers are written so they can be read from the bottom or the right of the sheet. Smaller dimensions go nearer the view and larger ones outside them, so lines do not cross. Holes are dimensioned from a datum edge and shown with Ø for a diameter, and arcs with R for a radius.
markingPoints: Units in mm stated once; dimensions give the real size whatever the scale
Each size shown once only, and all needed sizes given
Placed outside the views, on the clearest view, not on hidden lines
Thin lines with a gap at the outline and a small overrun; neat arrowheads; readable numbers
Smaller inside larger; holes from a datum; Ø and R symbols used

essays.stem: Compare isometric and oblique drawings. Say how each is drawn and when each one is useful.
essays.modelAnswer: Both are pictorial drawings that show three faces of an object in one view, so they are easy for people to understand. In an isometric drawing the vertical edges stay vertical and the two sets of horizontal edges are drawn at 30° to the horizontal, using the 30°/60° set square. Sizes along these three axes are measured at their true length. Circles on any face become ellipses, which take time to draw well. Isometric gives a balanced, natural look, and it is useful for showing how a fabricated frame or bracket will look, or for assembly instructions. In an oblique drawing the front face is drawn in its true shape, like a front view, and the receding edges go back at 45°. In cabinet oblique the receding lines are drawn at half length so the object does not look too deep. Oblique is quicker when the front face has circles or curves, because they stay true circles. It is useful for parts such as flanges or plates with holes.
markingPoints: Both are pictorial and show three faces in one view
Isometric: verticals stay vertical, other edges at 30°, true lengths along the axes
Isometric circles become ellipses; good balanced look for frames and assemblies
Oblique: front face true shape, receding lines at 45° (half length in cabinet oblique)
Oblique useful for parts with circles or curves on the front face

essays.stem: Explain why sectional views are used, and describe how to draw a full section through a part such as a pipe flange, including the hatching rules.
essays.modelAnswer: A sectional view shows the inside of a part as if it had been cut through and the front piece taken away. It is used when the inside has holes, bores or recesses that would only show as many confusing hidden lines. To draw a full section of a flange, first show the cutting plane on another view, such as the end view, as a thin chain line with thick ends, with arrows to show the direction of looking and letters such as A–A. Then draw the sectional view in place of the outside view, showing the outline of the cut faces and any edges seen beyond the cut, such as the far side of the bolt holes. Hidden lines are usually left out. The cut surfaces are hatched with thin lines at 45°, evenly spaced about 3–4 mm apart. All the hatching on one part goes the same way; on a different part next to it, it goes the other way. Shafts, bolts, nuts and thin ribs cut along their length are not hatched. Label the view, for example SECTION A–A.
markingPoints: Purpose: shows the inside clearly instead of many hidden lines
Cutting plane shown as a thin chain line, thick at the ends, with arrows and letters
Section drawn with the cut faces and edges beyond; hidden lines usually left out
Hatching thin at 45°, evenly spaced, one direction per part, opposite on the next part
Shafts, bolts, nuts and ribs cut lengthways not hatched; view labelled

essays.stem: Describe four types of line used on mechanical drawings: how each one looks and what each is used for.
essays.modelAnswer: A thick continuous line is used for visible outlines and edges, the parts of the object you can see in that view. It is the darkest line on the drawing. A thin continuous line is used for dimension lines, projection lines, leader lines and hatching, so that these do not get mixed up with the outline. A thin dashed line, made of short dashes with small, even gaps, shows hidden edges and holes that are behind the surface you are looking at. A thin chain line, a long dash then a dot, is used for centre lines through holes, arcs and round parts, and for lines of symmetry. A centre line should go a little past the outline. A thin chain line that is thick at its ends and where it changes direction shows a cutting plane for a section. A thin wavy freehand line shows where part of a view has been broken off to save space. Using the right line types means anyone can read the drawing in the same way.
markingPoints: Thick continuous — visible outlines and edges
Thin continuous — dimension, projection and leader lines, hatching
Thin dashed — hidden edges and features
Thin chain — centre lines and lines of symmetry
Clear description of how each line looks, or a correct further type (cutting plane, break line)

essays.stem: Explain how to draw a regular hexagon with a compass and rule when you know the distance across its corners, and say where hexagons are seen on mechanical drawings.
essays.modelAnswer: The distance across the corners of a regular hexagon is the diameter of a circle that passes through all six corners. Draw a horizontal and a vertical centre line crossing at the centre. Set the compass to half the across-corners distance, which is the radius, and draw the circle. Without changing the compass, put its point where the circle meets the horizontal centre line, and step the radius round the circle, making a mark each time. The radius fits exactly six times around the circle, because a regular hexagon is made of six equal triangles. Join the six marks with straight lines using the rule, and line them in. Check that each side is the same length and that opposite sides are parallel. Hexagons are seen on drawings of nuts and bolt heads, and of hexagon bar. Their size is often given across the flats, the distance between two opposite flat sides, which is smaller than the distance across the corners.
markingPoints: Across corners is the diameter of a circle through the corners; centre lines and circle drawn
Compass set to the radius and stepped six times round the circle
Reason: the hexagon is six equal (equilateral) triangles
Marks joined; sides equal and opposite sides parallel
Used for nuts, bolt heads and hexagon bar; size often given across the flats

essays.stem: Explain how to measure a real part in the workshop and make a freehand sketch that someone else could use to produce a scale drawing.
essays.modelAnswer: First look at the part and decide which views are needed to show every feature, usually a front view, a plan and an end view, or a pictorial sketch with extra views. Clean the part so that the edges and holes can be seen. Sketch the views freehand on squared or plain paper with a soft pencil, keeping the proportions about right, and leave space around each view for the dimensions. Add centre lines through the holes. Then measure the part with suitable tools: a steel rule or tape for lengths, a vernier caliper for thicknesses, hole sizes and small distances, and a protractor for angles. Measure from one edge or datum where possible. Write every size on the sketch as you measure it, with dimension lines and arrows, so that nothing has to be guessed later. Note the material, the thickness, any welds, the number needed, and your name and the date. Check the sketch against the part once more before you put it away.
markingPoints: Chooses the views needed and leaves space for dimensions
Freehand views in good proportion, with centre lines
Measures with suitable tools (rule, tape, vernier caliper, protractor), from a datum
Every size written on as it is measured
Material, quantity, welds, name and date noted; sketch checked against the part

essays.stem: Describe how a drawing should be checked, approved, issued and changed, and explain why this control matters.
essays.modelAnswer: When the drawing is finished, the drafter checks it first: every view, line type, size and note, against the sketch or design. Then another competent person, such as the supervisor or instructor, checks it again, because it is hard to see your own mistakes. They look for missing or repeated sizes, sizes that do not add up, the wrong projection, and errors in the title block. When it is correct, the checker signs and dates the title block and the drawing is approved. Copies are issued to the people who need them, such as the workshop, and the issue is recorded in a drawing register. If the design changes later, the drawing is updated, the revision letter and date are changed, and a note says what was changed. New copies are issued, and the old copies are taken back or clearly marked as out of date. This control matters because a wrong or old drawing can lead to parts being made wrongly, wasting time and material, or to unsafe work.
markingPoints: Self-check, then a check by another competent person
Checker looks for missing, repeated or wrong sizes and title block errors; signs and dates
Issued copies recorded in a register
Changes: revision letter and date updated, change noted, new copies issued, old ones withdrawn
Why it matters: old or wrong drawings cause wasted work, wrong parts or unsafe work

practical1.title: Three-view orthographic working drawing of a welded bracket on A3
practical1.brief: Each member of the group makes one working drawing by hand of a welded bracket, from a model or an isometric picture that the instructor gives the group. Use A3 paper, a scale of 1:1 or 1:2, and the projection the instructor names (first-angle or third-angle). Draw a border and title block, then the front view, plan and end view, with the correct line types, centre lines, dimensions and the projection symbol. When the drawings are finished, members swap drawings, check each other's work with the group's checking list, and write any corrections on a sticky note on the drawing. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group, with every member's drawing.
materials: A3 drawing paper and drafting tape
Drawing board and T-square (or a drawing table with a parallel motion)
45° and 30°/60° set squares, protractor and scale rule
2H and HB pencils, eraser and soft brush
Compass, dividers and a circle template
A model or isometric picture of a welded bracket, with sizes
A simple checking list and sticky notes
photos: Each sheet fixed square, with the border and title block drawn
Light construction lines blocking in the three views
The views lined in, before the dimensions are added
A finished, dimensioned drawing with the projection symbol and title block filled in
Members checking each other's drawings with the checking list
All the members' drawings laid out together, with their names showing
checklist: Fixed the sheet square and drew a neat border and title block
Chose a scale and spaced the views to fit the sheet
Placed the views correctly for the projection named, lined up with projection lines
Used the correct line types: thick outlines, thin dashed hidden lines, thin chain centre lines
Dimensioned the part fully, each size once, in mm, outside the views where possible
Filled in the title block, including the scale and the projection symbol
Checked another member's drawing and noted any errors clearly
safety: Keep compass and divider points covered or pointing down when not in use
Sit at a comfortable height with good light, and take short breaks
Keep the drawing area tidy and free of drinks
Carry boards and T-squares carefully so they do not strike others

practical2.title: Measure and sketch a workshop part, then make an isometric drawing of it
practical2.brief: As a group, choose a simple fabricated part from the workshop that the instructor approves, such as a welded tool holder, a small bracket or a vice jaw cover. Every member measures the part, makes their own freehand sketch with three views and all the sizes, and then makes an isometric drawing of it on A3 or A4 paper at a stated scale, using instruments. Members take turns with the measuring tools and check each other's sizes. Show at least one hole or curve as an ellipse on the isometric drawing. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group, with every member's sketch and drawing.
materials: A simple fabricated part from the workshop
Steel rule, tape measure, vernier caliper and protractor
Squared paper for sketches, and A3 or A4 drawing paper
Drawing board, T-square, 30°/60° set square and scale rule
2H and HB pencils, eraser, compass and an ellipse or circle template
photos: The part, with group members measuring it
A member's freehand sketch with all the sizes written on
The isometric construction lines (the box) on the sheet
A finished isometric drawing, with an ellipse for a hole or curve
Every member's sketch and isometric drawing laid out beside the part
checklist: Measured the part accurately with suitable tools, from a datum
Sketch shows the needed views in good proportion, with all sizes written on
Drew the isometric axes correctly: verticals vertical, other edges at 30°
Measured along the isometric axes to the stated scale
Drew holes or curves as neat ellipses on the right faces
Lined in the drawing clearly and added a title, the scale and their name
Shared the measuring tools and checked another member's sizes
safety: Handle the workshop part with care; check it for sharp edges and burrs
Keep compass points covered when not in use
Sit with good posture and good light, and take short breaks
Return measuring tools clean to their cases
